entries.name: Jaguar
behaviour: ambushes at forest streams and riverbanks
swims and climbs with ease
punctures skulls and turtle shells with a crushing bite, the strongest of any big cat for its size
entries.notes: The Americas' apex cat. Hunts from the riverbank; a player crossing a stream at night is exactly in its ambush lane.

entries.name: Bornean orangutan
behaviour: builds a fresh sleeping nest in the canopy every night
essentially solitary; only mothers with young stay together
flanged males give long-distance calls and long calls summon females
entries.notes: Critically endangered and the slowest-reproducing great ape; the face people picture when they imagine 'ape in the jungle'.

entries.name: Western lowland gorilla
behaviour: silverback leads the troop
knuckle-walks
chest-beating display and mock charges intimidate rather than attack
builds ground or low-nest sleeping platforms
entries.notes: The heavyweight of the gorillas; habituated gorilla families reward patient filming more than confrontation.

entries.name: Common chimpanzee
behaviour: fission-fusion parties constantly merge and split
uses tools: fishes termites, cracks nuts with stones, sponges water with leaves
communities conduct coordinated hunts and border patrols that can be lethal
entries.notes: Closest relative for behavior: tools, politics and warfare. Depict them as individuals with memories, not scenery.

entries.name: White-handed gibbon
behaviour: fiercely pair-bonded, one territory pair plus offspring
male and female duet with elaborate dawn songs that carry for kilometres
moves almost entirely by brachiation, swinging arm over arm beneath branches
entries.notes: The forest's dawn choir. In-game, its song is the cheapest way to make a rainforest feel inhabited at a distance.

entries.name: Proboscis monkey
behaviour: males grow huge pendulous noses used to amplify calls and impress females
excels at swimming, leaping straight into rivers from the canopy
troops favour mangrove and river-edge forest
entries.notes: Unmistakable Borneo endemic; the only primate that leaps from trees into rivers to escape.

entries.name: Mantled howler monkey
behaviour: howls at dawn and dusk; the call carries over 3 km through the canopy
spends most of the day motionless, digesting tough leaves
prehensile tail works as a fifth limb
entries.notes: Leaf-eater that conserves energy by doing almost nothing; its pre-dawn roar defines the soundtrack.

entries.name: Black-handed spider monkey
behaviour: fission-fusion bands of up to 40 split and reunite through the day
no opposable thumbs; swings like a living cable beneath limbs
key seed disperser: defecates seeds far from the parent tree
entries.notes: The acrobat of the canopy; fast-moving dark shapes against the light, always more legs than expected.

entries.name: Capybara
behaviour: world's largest rodent
semiaquatic: grazes ashore by day, escapes into water at the first sign of danger
lives in herds along riverbanks and eats water plants most vertebrates ignore
entries.notes: The all-purpose prey of every South American predator; model herds clustered on banks, bursting into water together.

entries.name: White-lipped peccary
entries.migrates: follows fruiting palms across the forest
behaviour: nomadic herds of up to 300 march for kilometres on palm-fruit quests
musk gland above the tail floods a groun with its scent
defensive circle around young when alarmed, tusks out
entries.notes: Pig-like but not a pig; a herd of 200 shouldering through the undergrowth is a wall, not a group.

entries.name: Lowland tapir
behaviour: prehensile snout hoovers up fallen fruit and aquatic plants
wallows in rivers and floods to cool and shed parasites
moves between feeding trees on established night trails
entries.notes: South America's largest land mammal; a living seed-disperser every rainforest depends on.

entries.name: Baird's tapir
behaviour: reclusive and nocturnal; usually seen before it is heard
swims and floats half-submerged to reach bank vegetation
adults are effectively black; young are striped white and brown
entries.notes: National mammal of Belize; the biggest native land herbivore between Mexico and Colombia.

entries.name: Brown-throated sloth
behaviour: hangs upside down; fur hosts algae that camouflages it
descends to defecate once a week in the same dung-clearing
slow metabolism makes it hard for eagles to spot, except on the ground
entries.notes: So slow that algae colonize its coat; at a distance it is a mossy lump that occasionally blinks.

entries.name: Ocelot
behaviour: solitary ambush hunter of the forest floor and low canopy
marks territory with scent and sharpened claws
dappled coat dissolves into leaf shadow
entries.notes: The housecat-sized assassin; if the player meets one in a dark corridor, it has every advantage.

entries.name: Kinkajou
behaviour: honey bear of the canopy with a prehensile tail and a long tongue for nectar
major pollinator of balsa and other night-blooming trees
sometimes raids tree cavities together; one female cares together with another
entries.notes: The 'honey bear' that is neither; slow-moving golden eyes at headlamp height.

entries.name: White-nosed coati
behaviour: female bands forage through leaf litter with upturned snouts
males solitary except in mating season
freezes then liquidates into trees when alarmed; descends headfirst
entries.notes: The raccoon-family troupe that turns up around ruins and campsites; bold, curious and quick to scatter.

entries.name: Sumatran tiger
behaviour: solitary ambush predator; launches in a 15 m bound
powerful swimmer; patrols rivers and ridge lines
stripes vanish into dim green light at dusk
fewer than 400 remain; they are forest ghosts
entries.notes: The only island tiger; the last big predator of Sumatra, encountered mostly as fresh pugmarks.

entries.name: Okapi
behaviour: giraffe's only living relative, retiring into Ituri forest
white-striped haunches flash in leaf shadow to confuse predators
prehensile dark-blue tongue strips leaves like a giraffe
leaves its hidden calf alone for up to 80% of the first two months
entries.notes: Unknown to science until 1901. Encountering one is a badge of deep-Congoil exploration.

entries.name: Sumatran rhinoceros
behaviour: smallest and hairiest of the rhinos; two small horns
solitary browser wandering steep ridge forest
wallows in mud wallows against biting flies
fewer than 80 confirmed alive; on the knife's edge of extinction
entries.notes: The rarest big mammal on Earth; the whole species could fit in one small room. Any specimen is a conservation emergency.

entries.name: Asian elephant
entries.migrates: seasonal between forest and crop fields
behaviour: smaller than African cousin; rounded ears and one finger-like trunk tip
forest and forest-edge grazing herds led by a matriarch
pushes over trees and digs roots; elephant paths become forest roads
young bulls in musth are unpredictable
entries.notes: The intelligent heavy machinery of the forest; crops raids put them on a collision course with farmers.

entries.name: Pygmy hippopotamus
behaviour: secretive and largely solitary, unlike river hippos
feeds on ferns and stream plants at night, hides in swamp by day
breathes with ears and nostrils sealed; plated armour under skin
found almost only in Liberia's Sapo National Park and neighbours
entries.notes: The wallet version of a hippo: Liberia's most elusive rainforest resident, rarely seen even by locals.

entries.name: Giant river otter
behaviour: family clans defend stretches of river and fish it cooperatively
constantly vocalizing: whistles, growls, hums and screams
cream throat patch is unique per individual
attacks anacondas and caimans in defense of kits
entries.notes: The loudest otter on Earth; a family clan patrolling a river bend will not be ignored.

entries.name: Scarlet macaw
behaviour: pairs mate for life and nest in high tree cavities
flocks gather at clay licks (collpas) to eat detoxifying clay
beak cracks palm nuts that nothing else can open
eggs incubated ~26 days
entries.notes: The rainforest's flying flag; flocks at the clay lick are the must-see spectacle of the lowlands.

entries.name: Keel-billed toucan
behaviour: enormous rainbow bill is lightweight honeycomb bone, used to reach and toss fruit
nests in natural tree cavities abandoned by woodpeckers
pairs stay together year-round
eggs incubated ~16 days
entries.notes: Belize's national bird; the bill looks impossible but is lighter than it appears.

entries.name: Harpy eagle
behaviour: double-crested crown flattens when alarmed
talons on a monkey arm can lift a 9 kg prey and barely slow it
nests in emergent trees 30-43 m up; a nest stick cradle reused for decades
incubation ~55 days
entries.notes: The canopy assassin; the only predator that routinely drops sloths out of high branches.

entries.name: Southern cassowary
entries.migrates: altitude seasonal movements between fruiting trees
behaviour: 5 cm dagger claw on inner toe can disembowel a person
male alone incubates eggs and raises striped chicks
swallows fruits larger than any other animal can; key disperser of rainforest giants
charges at movement, deflecting with head and casque
entries.notes: Often called the most dangerous bird alive; cross one at your own risk, it is bigger and faster than you.

entries.name: Greater bird-of-paradise
behaviour: males display on leks, fanning golden flank plumes into two meters of streamers
plumes drove a centuries-long global feather trade
lekking grounds shift between seasons
incubation ~18 days
entries.notes: The 'apoda' (footless) name comes from early Europeans removing the feet before mounting skins; feathers once worth a fortune.

entries.name: Green anaconda
behaviour: world's heaviest snake; females far larger than males
ambush beneath surface of swamps and still rivers, eyes and nostrils above water
constricts, then swallows prey whole over minutes to hours
breeding 'balls' of up to a dozen males coil around one female

voxel_model.pattern: rows of dark oval spots, double head stripe

entries.notes: Folklore made it monster-sized; reality (6-8 m, 100+ kg females) is still plenty. Wading deep swamp water is not advised.

entries.name: Boa constrictor
behaviour: ambush constrictor of branches and forest floor; juveniles hunt entirely arboreally
labial heat pits detect warm mammals in the dark
vibrates its tail as a decoy; ovoviviparous, gives live birth
roosts coiled in horizontal branches, motionless for weeks
entries.notes: The default big snake; solid, patterned and mostly interested in ignoring you.

entries.name: Emerald tree boa
behaviour: pure arboreal predator; hunts from a coiled branch perch
bright green with white lightning bolts; juveniles are orange or red before turning green
prehensile tail anchors the hunt
ovoviviparous, giving live birth
entries.notes: A jewel that rarely moves; the most beautiful snake any player will ever misjudge.

entries.name: Black caiman
entries.migrates: moves between lagoons in the dry season
behaviour: largest predator of the Amazon after the jaguar; up to six metres of muscle
nests a mound of vegetation; females guard the nest fiercely
skin hunted almost to extinction in the 1900s; making a slow comeback
basks on beaches at dawn; eyes glow at night
entries.notes: The old apex of the blackwater; the same bays that hide piranhas now hide one very patient crocodile.

entries.name: King cobra
behaviour: world's longest venomous snake; neurotoxic venom
the only snake that builds a nest of leaf litter, guarded by both parents
captures other snakes and swallows them whole
rises a metre above the ground when threatened
entries.notes: An intelligent, snake-eating serpent with parental care; the only cobra that genuinely hunts other snakes.

entries.name: Red-eyed tree frog
behaviour: sleeps folded on leaf edges by day; red eyes flash open at night
females lay eggs on leaves overhanging ponds; tadpoles drop into the water when rain starts
vertical pupils and orange feet grip waxy leaves
entries.notes: The poster frog; a leaf that suddenly blinks red.

entries.name: Strawberry poison-dart frog
behaviour: alkaloid venom from ant diet; captive-bred frogs are harmless
females carry tadpoles on their backs and feed them unfertilised eggs
aposematic morphs range from plain red to blue-legged to speckled

voxel_model.pattern: red body with blue-black legs (varies by island)

entries.notes: Technically edible if you raised it in captivity, technically suicidal to taste one from the leaf litter.

entries.name: Red-bellied piranha
behaviour: shoals of 20-100 for feeding and defense
legendary frenzies are mostly scavenging triggered by blood and thrashing
razor triangular teeth lock unilaterally for a bone-shearing bite
opportunistic; plants and fruit are real menu items too
entries.notes: The school is the unit: one piranha is a bite, a hundred is an incident.

entries.name: Amazon river dolphin
entries.migrates: into flooded forest (igapós) when rains raise the river
behaviour: adult males blush pink from blood vessels near the skin
unfused neck vertebrae let it turn its head in cluttered flooded forest
uses sonar clicks to hunt in black water
folklore: the boto shape-shifts into a handsome stranger at night
entries.notes: One of two riverine cetaceans; the flooded-forest maze is its natural hunting ground.

entries.name: Arapaima
behaviour: air-breather: must surface every 5-15 minutes; gulps loudly
one of the world's largest freshwater fish, historically to 3 m and 200 kg
bony tongue plates grind prey; armour-scaled like a Roman shield
parental care: males build and guard shallow nests

voxel_model.pattern: red-edged scales on rear flanks and tail

entries.notes: Managed by fisheries in parts of the Amazon; a lung-fishing trophy and a protein staple.

entries.name: Leafcutter ant
behaviour: colonies of millions farm a fungus on chewed leaf pulp; they never eat the leaves directly
castes range from tiny nurses to soldiers with heads bigger than a berry
trails of green fragments march overhead like living conveyor belts
a mature nest can clear ~0.5 ha of vegetation
entries.notes: Earth's most successful farmers before humans; the main defoliator of the forest.

entries.name: Goliath birdeater
behaviour: world's largest spider by mass; leg span to 28 cm
flicks barbed urticating hairs from its abdomen when threatened
stridulates: a loud hiss from rubbing fang bases
digs a deep burrow in the forest floor and waits
entries.notes: Despite the name it almost never eats birds; the hairs are the real weapon, not the venom.
